Highlights • Feasibility of multiplexed blood-based protein levels in sport-related concussion. • Identify novel blood-based biomarkers for concussed athletes. • Dysregulation of blood-based proteins provides a better understanding of human response to injury. • EPB41 and alpha synuclein distinguish concussed athletes from non-concussed athletes. Background Current protein biomarkers are only moderately predictive at identifying individuals with mild traumatic brain injury or concussion. Therefore, more accurate diagnostic markers are needed for sport-related concussion. Methods This was a multicenter, prospective, case-control study of athletes who provided blood samples and were diagnosed with a concussion or were a matched non-concussed control within the National Collegiate Athletic Association–Department of Defense Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education Consortium conducted between 2015 and 2019. The blood was collected within 48 h of injury to identify protein abnormalities at the acute and subacute timepoints. Athletes with concussion were divided into 6 h post-injury (0–6 h post-injury) and after 6 h post-injury (7–48 h post-injury) groups. We applied a highly multiplexed proteomic technique that used a DNA aptamers assay to target 1305 proteins in plasma samples from athletes with and without sport-related concussion. Results A total of 140 athletes with concussion (79.3% males; aged 18.71 ± 1.10 years, mean ± SD) and 21 non-concussed athletes (76.2% males; 19.14 ± 1.10 years) were included in this study. We identified 338 plasma proteins that significantly differed in abundance (319 upregulated and 19 downregulated) in concussed athletes compared to non-concussed athletes. The top 20 most differentially abundant proteins discriminated concussed athletes from non-concussed athletes with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.954 (95% confidence interval: 0.922‒0.986). Specifically, after 6 h of injury, the individual AUC of plasma erythrocyte membrane protein band 4.1 (EPB41) and alpha-synuclein (SNCA) were 0.956 and 0.875, respectively. The combination of EPB41 and SNCA provided the best AUC (1.000), which suggests this combination of candidate plasma biomarkers is the best for diagnosing concussion in athletes after 6 h of injury. Conclusion Our data suggest that proteomic profiling may provide novel diagnostic protein markers and that a combination of EPB41 and SNCA is the most predictive biomarker of concussion after 6 h of injury. molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Sport-related concussion (SRC), mild traumatic brain injuries (mTBIs), neuronal injury, and physiological stress.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The study identifies dysregulation of blood-based proteins as key to understanding human response to injury following SRC. Candidate biomarkers like total tau, neurofilament light, GFAP, and UCH-L1 are associated with neuronal, axonal, and astroglial damage post-mTBI. EPB41, an erythrocyte isoform expressed in the brain, is crucial for CNS function, stabilizing the spectrin-actin cytoskeleton. SNCA, a presynaptic neuronal protein, is involved in synaptic plasticity and dopamine regulation; its dysregulation is linked to neuronal damage, reflecting injury after SRC. Cardiac-related proteins (Troponin T, I, FABP3) indicate myocardial cell damage and are associated with physiological stress post-SRC. FABP3, also present in dopaminergic neurons, regulates fatty acid metabolism and can stimulate SNCA oligomerization and accumulation, leading to dopaminergic neuron toxicity and neurodegeneration.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study did not involve dose comparison but focused on temporal dynamics of protein abundance post-injury. Athletes were divided into acute (0–6 hours) and subacute (7–48 hours) phases post-concussion. Within the first 6 hours, 66 proteins were differentially abundant but not significant after multiple comparison correction, requiring cautious interpretation. After 6 hours (7–48 h), 694 proteins were differentially abundant (624 more, 70 less abundant), indicating time-dependent proteomic changes. Subgroup analysis for candidate biomarkers within 6 hours did not show significant differentiation after adjustment.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The combination of EPB41 and SNCA demonstrated the highest specificity for diagnosing concussion, achieving an AUC of 1.000 after 6 hours post-injury. A single EPB41 marker had an AUC of 0.956 in this timeframe. While the SomaScan assay uses aptamers with high affinity and specificity for protein targets, the diagnostic ability of acute phase proteins (within 6h post-injury) to differentiate concussion was not established. It was noted that cardiac muscle-specific enzymes (Troponin T, I, FABP3) can be elevated in severe TBI and stroke patients without cardiac injury, indicating their lack of sole specificity to cardiac damage and broader implications in neurological trauma.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Collegiate athletes (aged 17–23 years, mean 18.76 ± 1.13 years), primarily White and non-Hispanic males, participating in contact sports, diagnosed with sport-related concussion (SRC) or mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI).
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Sport-related concussion is a significant public health concern linked to long-term symptoms. The identification of EPB41 and SNCA as novel candidate biomarkers offers crucial implications for improving the diagnosis of SRC and mTBI. These findings support the development of a diagnostic panel reflecting neuronal injury and physiological stress, although future studies are needed to determine their prognostic value.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility for sport-related concussion and mild traumatic brain injury.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The combination of EPB41 and SNCA showed high diagnostic accuracy and reliability for concussion diagnosis after 6 hours post-injury, achieving an AUC of 1.000, which is comparable to clinical assessment (SCAT-3 AUC = 0.938). Individual AUCs were 0.956 for EPB41 and 0.875 for SNCA in this timeframe. In contrast, results for proteins differentially abundant within 6 hours post-injury were not significant after multiple comparison correction and should be interpreted cautiously. This study utilized a highly sensitive SomaScan proteomic assay, moving beyond limited accuracy of previous hypothesis-driven studies. Limitations include varied blood draw times (0-48h), small sample size, predominantly White and non-Hispanic male participants limiting generalizability, potential for unrecorded sub-concussive hits, and possible unidentified SRC in the control group.
recommended_alternatives: The study identifies EPB41 and alpha-synuclein (SNCA) as the most predictive diagnostic protein markers for concussion. It implicitly suggests further investigation into the other 338 differentially abundant proteins identified by proteomic profiling for potential additional markers. Additionally, the study recommends a non-hypothesis-based, data-driven proteomic profiling approach for biomarker discovery and highlights previously unconsidered proteins as new diagnostic candidates. Future research should determine their clinical utility in larger, more inclusive cohorts (diverse sports and populations) and validate them, as well as focus on determining the prognostic value of the identified biomarkers. Previously considered biomarkers like total tau, neurofilament light, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase-L1 (UCH-L1) are also mentioned in the context of mTBI but not as direct alternatives to EPB41/SNCA in this study's primary recommendation.
